newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries bullish but wary of "Super Friday".
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries bullish but wary of "Super Friday".

text.p: Recent economic data have given U.S. Treasury market bulls plenty of reasons to celebrate, but analysts warned that some key indicators on Friday could spoil the party.

In a rare combination of events, two of America's most-watched indicators -- the employment report and the National Association of Purchasing Management index -- will be released on what market players are calling a "Super Friday."

The market hopes the non-farm payrolls report -- seen as the most important release of the day -- will shed some light on an economic scenario that has otherwise been characterized by its lack of a clear trend.
But given the Treasury market recent rally, analysts said they see little room for a sharp rise in prices.
"The risk is that you could be setting yourself up for a little bit more of a disappointment on Friday," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and economist at Dean Witter Reynolds.
Analysts said the market now needs further evidence of a slowing economy before it rises again.

"The market has rallied this week and it will take more evidence of economic weakness to send yields down further," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank. "We actually expect some profit-taking if the numbers come in as expected."
In a Reuters survey, Wall Street pundits expect non-farm payrolls to rise by 212,000 in October against a 40,000 drop the previous month. The unmemployment rate is seen unchanged at 5.2 percent.
Average hourly earnings are seen up 0.4 percent against 0.5 percent jump in September, while the average work week is seen rising to 35.9 hours from 34.7 hours earlier.
Treasury prices rose sharply earlier in the week after the Employment Cost Index (ECI) for the third quarter rose 0.6 percent, below an expected 0.8 percent increase.
The rally brought the yield on the benchmark 30-year bond below 6.70 percent and to its lowest level since April.
Analysts said a weaker than expected payroll report could send the T-bond yield down to as low as 6.50 percent, while a stronger than expected number could bring the yield back up to 6.80 percent.
"The payrolls will be the most important report," said William Dudley, senior economist at Goldman Sachs and Co. Inc.
"The payrolls are a broader measure of how the economy is doing and also the key question in the market's mind is what is happening to consumer spending now," Dudley added.
Market players will also be keeping an eye on the NAPM report. Economists in a Reuters poll see the index falling slightly to 51 in October against 51.7 in the previous month.
"The NAPM will probably not carry as much weight coming out after the employment report," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
"The reason is that NAPM is used by a lot of people in the market to try and predict what the employment report will look like," Low added.
Analysts also said the effects of a General Motors Corp strike on the NAPM report were still unclear, making the data even more difficult to gauge.
The GM workers strike started in Canada, but the lack of supply forced some U.S. plants to shut down as well.
"You've already seen some signs from trade reports suggesting a pull-back in auto and truck production from this strike," Dean Witter's Flanagan said.
In addition to the payrolls and NAPM reports, the market will also digest the September leading indicators and factory orders reports on Friday.
